\chapter{Two Things at Once}
\label{ch:bn-two-things-at-once}
\hlchaptermodality{28}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can put two nouns in one sentence with \bn{আর}, mark either of them with -\bn{ও}, offer a choice between them with \bn{বা}, and refuse both with \bn{না} … \bn{না}.}

The colours, foods and family words of eleven earlier chapters, joined two at a time for the first time: added with \bn{আর}, marked with -\bn{ও}, offered with \bn{বা}, and refused with \bn{না} … \bn{না}.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ār]{\bn{আর} (ār) — and}

\label{lesson:BN-C17-ar}



\begin{quote}
The chapter before this one gave you three ways to deny a sentence. This chapter gives you the first way to make a sentence longer than one idea.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the missing-thing negator — \emph{nei}
  \item \emph{Recall:} five chapters back, the first two colours — \emph{lāl}, \emph{nīl}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{আর}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{চা} \bn{আর} \bn{দুধ}} — \emph{chā ār dudh} — \textbf{tea and milk.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{চা} \bn{আর} \bn{জল} \bn{নেই}} — \emph{āmār chā ār jôl nei.} — \textbf{I have no tea and no water.}
\end{quote}

This book has taught four foods, four garments, five colours, four family words and four parts of the body — a hundred and thirty-nine lessons of nouns that could only ever be named one at a time. \textbf{\bn{আর}} is the word that ends that.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{আর}} comes from Sanskrit \emph{apara}, \textquotedblleft{}the other one, the further one\textquotedblright{} — so the joining sense grew out of a counting sense, \emph{one more}. It still carries that older meaning when it stands in front of a noun on its own: \textbf{\bn{আর} \bn{চা}}, \emph{more tea}. Chapter seven's \textbf{\bn{আবার}} (\emph{ābār}, \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}) is built on the same idea of one more time, which is why the two words sound like relatives. They are.

Bengali also writes \emph{ebông} for \emph{and} in formal prose. It joins clauses more than nouns, and it needs a letter this book has not taught yet, so it is named here in romanization — \emph{ebông} — and left for the script chapters.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chā ār dudh}
  \item \emph{jôl ār bhāt} — water and rice
  \item \emph{lāl ār nīl} — red and blue
  \item \emph{āmār chā ār jôl nei}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \textbf{\bn{আর}} mean before it meant \emph{and}? (\textbf{More, the other one} — Sanskrit \emph{apara}.) Which word taught in chapter seven is its relative? (\textbf{\bn{আবার}}, \emph{again} — one more time.) And what happens to a negator when two nouns are joined? (\textbf{Nothing} — it still sits at the end.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-o]{-\bn{ও} (-o) — the joiner that is one vowel long}

\label{lesson:BN-C17-o}



\begin{quote}
The lesson before this taught \textbf{\bn{আর}}, which stands between two things. This one goes on the end of one thing, and means much the same.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the letter chapter ten taught standing alone — \textbf{\bn{ও}}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: -\bn{ও}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{আমিও}} — \emph{āmi-o} — \textbf{me too.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{আমিও} \bn{ভালো}} — \emph{āmi-o bhālo.} — \textbf{I am well too.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{-\bn{ও}} never stands by itself. It is written onto the back of the word it attaches to, and it means \emph{that one as well}. Where \textbf{\bn{আর}} joins two nouns from between them, \textbf{-\bn{ও}} marks each of them from behind: \textbf{\bn{ভাই} \bn{আর} \bn{বোন}} is \emph{brother and sister}; \textbf{\bn{ভাইও} \bn{বোনও}} is \emph{the brother as well, and the sister as well}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the smallest word does the most work}]
Attaching \textbf{-\bn{ও}} to a different word moves the emphasis without moving a syllable of the sentence:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{said} & \textbf{means} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\bn{আমিও} \bn{ভালো}} & \emph{I too} am well — somebody else is as well \\
\textbf{\bn{আমি} \bn{ভালোও}} & I am well \emph{as well as} whatever else I am \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English has to say \emph{too} at the end and hope, or move the stress with the voice. Bengali puts the mark exactly on the word it belongs to. This is Sanskrit \emph{api}, \textquotedblleft{}also\textquotedblright{} — the particle Hindi still says whole as \emph{bhī}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āmi-o} — me too
  \item \emph{āmi-o bhālo}
  \item the pair joined both ways — \emph{bhāi ār bon}, then \emph{bhāi-o bon-o}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \textbf{-\bn{ও}} stand, and where does \textbf{\bn{আর}} stand? (\textbf{-\bn{ও}} on the back of a word; \textbf{\bn{আর}} between two of them.) Can \textbf{-\bn{ও}} be said on its own? (\textbf{No} — it has no life apart from the word it rides.) Which Hindi word is its cousin? (\emph{\textbf{bhī}}, from the same Sanskrit \emph{api}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bā]{\bn{বা} (bā) — or}

\label{lesson:BN-C17-ba}



\begin{quote}
Two joiners so far, and both of them add. Name them, and say which one stands between and which one hangs off the back.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{বা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{চা} \bn{বা} \bn{দুধ}} — \emph{chā bā dudh} — \textbf{tea or milk.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{চা} \bn{বা} \bn{দুধ}?} — \emph{chā bā dudh?} — \textbf{tea or milk?}
\end{quote}

Until this lesson nothing in this book could offer anybody a choice. \textbf{\bn{আর}} gives them both; \textbf{\bn{বা}} makes them pick. It sits exactly where \textbf{\bn{আর}} sits, between the two things, and nothing else in the sentence changes.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{বা}} is Sanskrit \emph{vā}, and it is one of the oldest unchanged words in this book: the same particle survives at the end of Latin \emph{sīve} (\textquotedblleft{}or if\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{neve} (\textquotedblleft{}nor\textquotedblright{}). Four thousand years and one syllable.

Put it inside the rising question this chapter's neighbour taught and you have the whole shape of an offer: two nouns, \textbf{\bn{বা}} between them, and a voice that goes up at the end. That is how tea gets poured.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chā bā dudh}
  \item the same pair joined instead of split — \emph{chā ār dudh}
  \item \emph{bhāt bā jôl} — rice or water
  \item it as an offer, with the voice rising — \emph{chā bā dudh?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which joiner adds and which one chooses? (\textbf{\bn{আর}} adds; \textbf{\bn{বা}} chooses.) Where does \textbf{\bn{বা}} stand? (\textbf{Between the two things}, exactly where \textbf{\bn{আর}} does.) And what turns an offer into a question? (\textbf{The rising voice} — nothing is added.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nā … nā …]{\bn{না} … \bn{না} … — neither, nor}

\label{lesson:BN-C17-na-na}



\begin{quote}
Chapter twenty-seven was firm about this: \textbf{\bn{না}} goes after. There is exactly one construction in which it goes first, and it is the one that denies both halves of a choice.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the word that offers the choice — \emph{bā}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{না} … \bn{না} …}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{না} \bn{চা}, \bn{না} \bn{দুধ}} — \emph{nā chā, nā dudh} — \textbf{neither tea nor milk.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{না} \bn{চা} \bn{আছে}, \bn{না} \bn{দুধ}} — \emph{āmār nā chā āchhe, nā dudh} — \textbf{I have neither tea nor milk.}
\end{quote}

One \textbf{\bn{না}} in front of each thing refused. The pattern is the mirror image of \textbf{\bn{আর}}: where \emph{and} stood once, between two nouns, \emph{neither} stands twice, before each of them.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three ways to refuse two things}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{shape} & \textbf{how it refuses} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\bn{আমার} \bn{চা} \bn{আর} \bn{দুধ} \bn{নেই}} & one negator at the end covers both \\
\textbf{\bn{চা}-\bn{ও} \bn{নেই}, \bn{দুধ}-\bn{ও} \bn{নেই}} & each thing marked with \textbf{-\bn{ও}}, each denied \\
\textbf{\bn{না} \bn{চা}, \bn{না} \bn{দুধ}} & the flat refusal, and the emphatic one \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

All three are correct Bengali. The first is what you say without thinking about it; the third is what you say when you want the refusal heard.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nā chā, nā dudh}
  \item the same refusal the ordinary way — \emph{āmār chā ār dudh nei}
  \item the marked way — \emph{chā-o nei, dudh-o nei}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \textbf{\bn{না}} stand in an ordinary negative sentence, and where in this one? (\textbf{After the verb} ordinarily; \textbf{in front of each refused thing} here.) Which joiner does the pattern mirror? (\textbf{\bn{আর}}, one \emph{and} between two becoming one \emph{no} before each.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ār · -o · bā]{Two things at once}

\label{lesson:BN-R17-joined-and-refused}



\begin{quote}
Three joiners landed in this chapter. Name them, and say for each one whether it adds, marks, or chooses.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} two colours joined — \emph{kālo ār shādā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the same two as a choice — \emph{kālo bā shādā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} yourself added to somebody — \emph{āmi-o}
  \item \emph{Say it:} both refused — \emph{nā kālo, nā shādā}
  \item \emph{Recall:} five lessons back, the negator for a verbless sentence — \emph{nôy}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which joiner turns a statement into an offer once the voice rises? (\textbf{\bn{বা}} — two things and a choice between them.) How many \textbf{\bn{না}} does a double refusal need, and where do they go? (\textbf{Two, one in front of each thing}.) And which of this chapter's joiners cannot stand on its own? (\textbf{-\bn{ও}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
